title: Plato's raised hand
hookLine: angry with a slave, Plato holds his raised hand in the air: I'm punishing an angry man (On Anger 3.12)

cards: A man stands in a room with his arm raised high, about to strike. He doesn't bring it down. He doesn't lower it either.
He just holds the pose, as if someone had pressed pause on him. A friend walks in and stares. What on earth are you doing?
The man is Plato, Socrates' student, and Seneca tells the story in On Anger, right after naming delay as the greatest remedy.

teach.b: First, the scene. Plato was furious with one of his slaves. He ordered the man to take off his tunic and bare his shoulders, and raised his hand to beat him himself.
Then, with his arm in the air, he realized he was angry. Second, the freeze. He didn't finish the blow, and he didn't drop his arm and pretend nothing had happened.
He stayed exactly where he was, holding the ugly pose.
When a friend asked what he was doing, Plato answered: I'm punishing an angry man. He'd forgotten the slave and found someone else to correct. Third, the handover.
After that, Seneca says, Plato took away his own power over his household.

teach.h: SPEUSIPPUS, YOU DO IT: I AM ANGRY.
teach.b: Once, upset over some offense, he told his student Speusippus: you beat this slave; I am angry. He refused to punish anyone while in that state. Fourth, the honest flinch, and the lesson.
This comes from a world where hitting a slave was ordinary, and even Plato's solution has someone else do it. It deserves a wince.

teach.h: THE MOMENT CAUGHT IN THE ACT.
teach.b: Seneca tells it for one reason: to show anger caught in the act.

The raised hand is the moment between impulse and action, frozen and made visible. That moment usually slips by unseen; by the time we notice, we're through it. Plato stopped in the middle and looked.
That frozen arm is what delay looks like from the outside.

how: Readers of On Anger sometimes practice freezing an angry gesture halfway, as Plato did, and refusing to correct anyone while still angry.

games.q: Plato's raised hand — tap the pairs.
p: asked to deal with the slave

s: Plato finished the blow and then apologized
he froze with his hand raised and never struck.
Plato once asked his student Speusippus to beat a slave for him because he was angry
he refused to punish anyone in that state.
Seneca tells the story to praise beating slaves calmly
he tells it to show anger caught in the act; the setting deserves a wince.

games.q: you're Plato. your hand is raised to strike, and you suddenly realize you're furious. what do you do?
o: freeze, and turn the correction on yourself.
drop your arm and pretend nothing happened.
games.why: he held the pose and told his friend: I'm punishing an angry man.

practice: Pick one of your own small angry gestures, a slammed cupboard, a sigh aimed at someone, a hard look, and gently make a soft version of it now: raise a hand, tighten your jaw.
Hold it, unfinished, and notice who you'd be punishing, and who actually needs correcting. Then let it go, slowly.

wordCard.voice: Irascor. Latin for 'I am angry': Plato's words when caught mid-blow, after which he refused to punish anyone while angry. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, 'I am angry': Plato's reason, in Seneca's telling, for handing the matter to someone else.

carryVoice: Your line: the raised hand. The pause can be caught, even halfway through. Five hundred five days in.
